meeting.title: Syncing CI YAML and project settings
meeting.credit: GitLab on YouTube: "Ops Cross-Stage Think Big - 2021-04-15" https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JaYXLlXrfDM

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: This is the OP section cross-stage Think Big for April 15th, 2021. Our topic today is one that I added to the agenda, so I'll be moderating today. I don't have a mural board for us, so we'll just be doing this discussion style

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: through the doc and verbally. I do have all of the prompt questions in the agenda if you want to click into that to follow along. But our topic today is one that has come up for the testing team a couple of times, and it's around settings, things that you can set up in CI/CD settings through the UI and things you can also do through your GitLab CI YAML file, how those things potentially are authored, displayed, conflict if that happens, and what we should do in those cases, understanding what the problem would be there.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: So that's our topic, and I've started with a problem description in kind of our jobs to be done style around, as a developer or a DevOps engineer who's setting up GitLab for my group, I want to know if there are conflicts between the GitLab CI YAML and settings so I can avoid hunting down questions from developers who have a bad experience, slash, I know, or I look like I know what I'm doing when it comes to GitLab.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: So that's what they're trying to accomplish in this. Um, specifically the one that comes up for us is around test coverage. You can set up your coverage badges, you can set up parsing for coverage in your settings in CI/CD. You can also do that at the job level in your GitLab CI YAML. Those two things could potentially be in conflict, and when that happens, it's not a great experience for a user.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: I have to imagine that this happens for in other areas of the site or for the platform. And so wanted to open it up to the broader group of how should we handle these things going forward.

chapters.title: Introduction to settings conflicts
chapters.gist: James introduces the problem of conflicting configurations between the UI settings and the GitLab CI YAML file.

chapters.title: Defining conflict examples
chapters.gist: The team discusses specific examples like pipeline success requirements and deploy freezes that cause user confusion.

chapters.title: Terraform and automation workflows
chapters.gist: Victor explains how infrastructure as code tools like Terraform complicate UI-based notifications and settings management.

chapters.title: Selecting a target persona
chapters.gist: The group debates whether to focus on the DevOps engineer making changes or the developer who encounters errors.

chapters.title: UX challenges in current settings
chapters.gist: Hyanna demonstrates the difficulty of finding related configurations across different parts of the project UI.

chapters.title: Brainstorming big picture outcomes
chapters.gist: The team explores automated solutions such as opening merge requests or creating to-dos when settings change.

chapters.title: Identifying technical blockers

chapters.title: Next steps and documentation

content.tldr: The team discussed the confusion caused when GitLab CI YAML files and project UI settings are out of sync. They explored ways to notify users of these conflicts or automate the alignment between the two configuration methods.

bullets.text: To address how settings in the UI and the CI YAML file can conflict or require dual updates.
Matching YAML logic with UI settings is technically complex and hard to automate perfectly.
The current UI makes it very difficult for users to find all the settings they need to enable a single feature.
Deploy freeze configurations requiring both UI and YAML changes.
The impact of merge request approval rules on developer workflows.
Identify specific settings for technical writers to update troubleshooting guides.
Create a consolidated epic to track the brainstormed ideas.

content.tldr: This session served as a conceptual review of configuration challenges in the Ops section. The team identified major technical and UX blockers before moving toward documentation-based iterations.

bullets.text: The team defined the core problem of configuration mismatch for various features like merge trains.
User permissions can prevent individuals from fixing conflicts between settings and code files.
Parsing the YAML and matching it to every possible UI setting is a huge technical hurdle.
The team decided to focus on low-hanging fruit like improved UI feedback and better documentation.
James will draft a consolidated issue to summarize the discussion and plan future work.

content.tldr: The team reviewed current pain points in the CI/CD configuration experience. They plan to gather data and update documentation to address these issues in the short term.

bullets.text: The testing team identified specific issues with coverage badge parsing and YAML conflicts.
Thao plans to identify specific settings her team owns that need better troubleshooting guides.
There is a lack of data on how often pipeline failures are caused by setting incompatibilities.

content.tldr: The group analyzed why current configuration workflows are confusing for both new and experienced users. They highlighted UI discoverability as a major area for improvement.

bullets.text: The group provided clear, real-world examples of where users feel pain during setup.
The team struggled to find specific settings during the meeting, illustrating the discoverability problem.
Automatically open a merge request to update the YAML file when a UI setting is changed.
Create to-dos for project owners when a YAML change requires a corresponding UI setting update.
